LPG 12kg cylinder price rises by Tk 252
item.description:
The price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplied by the private sector has increased at the consumer level. This time, the price has risen by Tk 21 per kilogramme.

As a result, the price of the most widely used 12kg LPG cylinder has increased by Tk 252, taking the new price to Tk 1,837 from Tk 1,585. The price had fallen by Tk 13 last month.

The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) announced the new price today, Sunday. The new price will take effect from 6:00 pm today. LPG prices rose in the wake of the outbreak of war in the Middle East.

LPG shortage as imports fall, prices rise

Following the start of a ceasefire, LPG prices began to decline on the international market. Prices had fluctuated over the past two months, but a significant surge has occurred again this month.

However, LPG supply in the market has remained below demand for the past three weeks. As a result, there have been allegations that 12kg LPG cylinders are being sold at Tk 500 to Tk 800 above the official price.

Earlier, LPG prices on the international market rose after the war spread across the Middle East. In April, the country recorded its highest-ever increase in LPG prices.

At the beginning of April, the price of a 12kg LPG cylinder was increased by Tk 387. It was raised by another Tk 212 on 19 April. However, prices fell for two consecutive months in June and July.

LPG import: BPC fails even after 7 months

According to BERC, LPG cylinders of various sizes are available in the market. From now on, the price of LPG will be Tk 153.06 per kilogramme. The prices of LPG cylinders of different sizes will be determined accordingly. Previously, the price was Tk 132.12 per kilogramme.

The commission determines LPG prices every month. However, LPG is not being sold in the market at the officially set prices. The 12kg LPG cylinder is the most widely used for household purposes.

There have been allegations that LPG sellers are charging customers more than the official price for each cylinder. Many people are turning to LPG cylinders for cooking at home amid the gas shortage.

The price of 12.5kg LPG cylinders supplied by state-owned companies has been kept unchanged at Tk 825. Meanwhile, the price of LPG used in vehicles, known as auto gas, has been set at Tk 84.62 per litre. Previously, it was Tk 73.09 per litre.

BERC has been setting LPG prices since April 2021. Propane and butane, the main components used to produce LPG, are imported from various countries. Every month, Saudi Arabian company Aramco publishes the prices of these two LPG components. This is known as the Saudi Contract Price (CP).

BERC adjusts LPG prices in Bangladesh based on this Saudi CP as the benchmark price. The commission calculates the average US dollar exchange rate for the entire month based on the invoice prices submitted by importing companies.

item.title: PM directs expediting Inner Circular Road project to ease Dhaka traffic
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Sunday asked the authorities concerned to expedite the construction of the inner circular road to ease traffic congestion in the capital.

He gave the instruction while chairing a meeting at his Office at the Bangladesh Secretariat to review progress in the construction of the Inner Circular Road in the capital, said PM's Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.

The prime minister asked the Road Transport and Bridges Ministry and the Local Government Division to jointly review the existing project plan and take steps to expedite the construction work.

The deputy press secretary said Tarique Rahman stressed identifying and removing the existing obstacles to implementing the project at the earliest, ensuring effective coordination among the agencies concerned and setting a realistic timeframe for completing the work.

He also asked the authorities to ensure visible progress in the project at the earliest.

Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for LGRD and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, State Minister for Road Transport and Bridges and Railways Habibur Rashid, Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Md Abdus Salam and Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton, among senior officials concerned, attended the meeting.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,125 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Sunday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,125.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,023, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 102, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the three new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with two deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 1,218 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Sunday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 196,418.
During the same period, 82 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 21,748.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 174,149 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 166,908 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Govt targets NPL recovery with new Distressed Asset Law
item.description:
The government is formulating a new legal framework titled the Distressed Asset Management Act, 2026 to accelerate the recovery of non-performing loans (NPLs) and manage long-stagnant assets in banks and non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs).
Stakeholder feedback on the draft has already been collected.
If a borrower fails to clear dues within a stipulated timeframe, specialized asset management companies will be empowered to seize and sell mortgaged collateral.
These entities can also purchase defaulted loans and distressed assets, restructure or securitize them, and assume operational control of defaulting businesses.
While finance ministry officials expect the framework to establish a specialized ecosystem for bad-asset resolution, economists warn that systemic challenges remain.
A substantial portion of defaulted loans lacks adequate collateral, while other securities are inflated up to four to five times their actual market value—making actual recovery difficult even after asset transfers.
A separate regulatory body—the Distressed Asset Management Unit (Damu)—will be set up in Dhaka under the administrative supervision of Bangladesh Bank, operating with functional autonomy.
To operate, DAMCs must be registered under the Companies Act, 1994, meet cash-paid-up capital requirements set by Damu, maintain strict "fit and proper" management standards, and ensure at least 20% independent directors on their boards.
DAMCs can purchase bad debts directly from financial institutions via bilateral contracts, paying the agreed purchase price entirely in cash.
DAMCs may raise funds locally or internationally by issuing shares, bonds, debentures, and security certificates, or through joint ventures with eligible institutional investors.
DAMCs can negotiate settlements, take physical possession of mortgaged assets, lease or sell property, convert debt into equity, and assume control of defaulting firms.
They can also extend loan tenures, reduce or waive interest, and haircut principal amounts (subject to Damu approval for major write-downs). Settled borrowers will receive "no-dues certificates."
Collateral market value will be assessed by Bangladesh Bank-approved valuers to determine a reserve price.
Borrowers will receive a 60-day notice to clear dues or redeem assets at the reserve price.
Failing this, assets will be sold via public tenders, open auctions, or bilateral agreements at or above the reserve price (or re-auctioned at up to a 10% discount if initial bids fall short).
If a borrower refuses to yield physical possession, District Magistrates or designated Executive Magistrates must enforce eviction and hand over assets within 15 working days.
Distressed assets can be placed into special-purpose trusts, insulating them from the general creditors of the DAMC or the selling financial institution.
Trust claims will hold first charge and priority over all debts, including government taxes and duties.
DAMCs and banks can hire licensed loan servicer companies to assist in borrower contact, restructuring, and asset tracing.
Servicers are strictly prohibited from taking deposits, conducting banking, or using coercive/illegal recovery tactics.
Restrictions and penalties
Defaulting borrowers and affiliated individuals are strictly barred from holding ownership, management, or board roles in DAMUS, DAMCs, or loan servicers, and cannot participate in asset auctions.

item.title: North Korea’s Kim oversaw launch of missile that uses AI
item.description:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch of a missile, which allegedly used artificial intelligence to adjust its trajectory, state media reported on Sunday.
The AI technology means the missile is “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude”, Kim’s powerful sister had said, adding this meant there was “no way to avoid” an attack.
It launched from an area around the eastern coastal city of Wonsan early Saturday morning and flew more than 700 kilometres , South Korea’s military said.
“Through today’s launching drill, the strategic missile soldiers have fully demonstrated their professional qualifications and counterattack posture,” Kim said after the launch, according to an English-language dispatch by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
“We must continue our responsible efforts nonstop to constantly and repeatedly make the enemy recognize the reliability and fatality of our strategic offensive means,” he added.
Seoul’s military disputed Kim’s sister’s remarks that there would be “no way to avoid” the projectile guided by AI, saying the missile launched on Saturday could have been intercepted.
“South Korea and the United States maintain a firm combined defence posture and assess that the missile recently launched by North Korea was well within the detection and interception capabilities of the defencive assets operated by the two allies,” Seoul’s defence ministry said in a statement.
“We urge North Korea to immediately cease actions that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula,” it said, adding that the launch violated UN Security Council resolutions.
The KCNA report disclosed the exact coordinates where the missile hit its target, a level of detail analysts said reflected Pyongyang’s “confidence”.
“This time, the North disclosed the coordinates down to decimal points -- equivalent to a precision of roughly 30 centimetres,” Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP.
“It shows Kim’s stance that there is nothing to hide and an expression of confidence.”
Photos released by KCNA showed a missile soaring into the sky in a burst of orange flame.
Another photo showed Kim smiling, flanked by his daughter Ju Ae and wife Ri Sol Ju, who is seen clapping her hands in celebration.
Ju Ae, who was first introduced to the public in 2022, is the most likely successor to her father, according to South Korea’s spy agency, citing her increasingly prominent role at major state and military events.
The launch was conducted to help train soldiers operating the “hypersonic strategic weapon system”, KCNA reported.

item.title: Imported fruits becoming a luxury in Bangladesh
item.description:
In Dhaka's market, the price of one kilogram of sweet orange (Malta) is currently Tk520 to Tk550.
During the same period, it sells for Tk100 to Tk160 in India, Tk80 to Tk130 in Pakistan, Tk130 to Tk180 in Nepal, and Tk300 to Tk400 in Sri Lanka.
This means the price of this fruit in Bangladesh is up to seven times higher than in neighboring countries.
This extreme price disparity is not limited to sweet oranges; a report by the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission highlights similar trends across various imported foreign fruits, including apples, oranges, grapes, and dates.
The report states that high customs duties, valuation at inflated prices during assessment, hyper-profit-seeking cartels among sellers, and the classification of fruit as a luxury item are driving foreign imported fruits to sell at abnormally high prices in the country.
Consequently, these fruits have slipped beyond the reach of ordinary consumers. Once regarded as essential diet for patients, these fruits have now become a heavy burden on consumers.
The report reveals that while apples sell for Tk350 to Tk450 per kg in the domestic market, the price per kg in India is only Tk220. In Pakistan, it is Tk170; in Nepal, Tk240; and in Sri Lanka, a maximum of Tk450.
A similar pattern was observed in the prices of oranges, grapes, and dates.
According to business sources and the government report, although fruit has played a key role in meeting essential nutritional needs for years, it was classified as a luxury product about two years ago.
High import taxes were subsequently imposed as a result.
Furthermore, Customs assesses duties based on values higher than the actual booking prices in the international market.
On the other hand, the market offers room for monopolistic practices. A limited group of importers handles these shipments, leaving the market reliant on them.
There is a widespread tendency among importers, wholesalers, and retailers to seek excessive profit margins when selling fruit.
Official categorizing
It is reported that in early September 2024, a circular issued by the Policy and Regulation Department of Bangladesh Bank categorized these fruits under luxury goods.
At the same time, it instructed imports to be conducted with a 100% margin requirement to protect the domestic fruit market. From that point on, fruit prices began to rise unchecked.
The Tariff Commission states that currently, import duties ranging from 96.10% to 121.78% are imposed on these fruit imports.
These include Customs Duty (CD), Supplementary Duty (SD), Value Added Tax (VAT), Advance Income Tax (AIT), Regulatory Duty (RD), and Advance Tax (AT).
In effect, almost every type of tax imaginable is levied on fruit imports.
Arbitrary valuation during assessment has further aggravated the crisis.
Considering urgent public health needs, Bangladesh Bank issued a circular in the middle of last month waiving the 100% margin reservation requirement for these fruit importers. However, heavy tariff rates on these items remain in force.
To resolve this situation, the Tariff Commission recommended several measures. Chief among them is the rationalization of the tariff structure.
The commission suggests removing fresh fruit and dates from the luxury goods list, reclassifying them as essential commodities, and withdrawing regulatory and supplementary duties.
Additionally, it recommended assessing customs valuation in line with international market rates and expediting clearance through a "Green Channel" due to the perishable nature of fresh fruit.
The commission also recommended easing LC (Letter of Credit) facilities for small and medium traders and expanding cold storage coverage.
Meanwhile, on Saturday (October 3), Commerce Minister Khondokar Abdul Muqtadir held an exchange-of-views meeting with traders and representatives of relevant government agencies to ensure adequate fruit supply and stabilize market prices.
Expressing dissatisfaction over the prices of imported fruits, including sweet oranges, he demanded an explanation from fruit traders on how the retail price per kilogram of sweet orange reaches Tk520 even after accounting for import costs, duties, taxes, and other expenses.
During the meeting, traders cited supply shortages.
They noted that high duties, transportation costs, shipping and port complications, and losses from previous shipments led many traders to reduce sweet orange imports. They added that as perishable goods, these fruits carry significant financial risks during transit and storage.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, a leader from the Bangladesh Fresh Fruits Importers Association told Dhaka Tribune that the government's calculations exist only on paper. We are facing actual losses in real business.
Furthermore, high profit-seeking is rampant not just at the import level, but among wholesalers and retailers as well—something the government has failed to control through proper market monitoring, he added.
SM Nazer Hossain, vice president of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told the media that some traders take advantage of dengue outbreaks to create artificial shortages and inflate fruit prices. Fruit prices systematically spike at this time of year when diseases peak, becoming a recurring pattern.
He noted that although the government reduced duties on fresh fruit imports as recently as March, prices rose instead of falling.
He urged the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and other relevant agencies to enforce strict oversight.

item.title: Envoy: EU sees Bangladesh as growing strategic partner
item.description:
The European Union views Bangladesh as a partner of growing strategic importance and wants to elevate ties beyond the traditional donor-recipient relationship, its ambassador said on Sunday.
Speaking at the Bay of Bengal Conversation in the capital, the Ambassador and Head of the EU Delegation to Bangladesh, Michael Miller, said the bloc was looking at Bangladesh with a "different level of ambition" British High Commissioner to Bangladesh Sarah Cook on Sunday met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and discussed the overall state of Bangladesh-UK relations, including prospects for greater trade and investment, economic cooperation and human resource development.
The meeting was held at the Prime Minister’s Office in the Cabinet Division of the Bangladesh Secretariat, said a press release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
During the meeting, they exchanged views on various issues of bilateral relations and matters of mutual interest.
They stressed the importance of further strengthening and broadening the longstanding and friendly relations between Bangladesh and the UK. The country approaches graduation from least developed country (LDC) status.
"We are looking at Bangladesh as a partner of growing strategic importance," he said while sharing his thoughts through the "Diplomatic Lens" at the international conference.
He described Bangladesh as a country of "scale, ambition and consequence", saying its importance extended across South Asia, the Bay of Bengal and the wider Indo-Pacific.
The envoy said the relationship was moving beyond the traditional donor-recipient framework that had characterized an important part of Bangladesh-EU cooperation over the past decades.
He acknowledged the contribution of the EU's Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preference scheme to Bangladesh's development progress, including its role in expanding employment opportunities for millions of people, particularly women.
As Bangladesh prepares for LDC graduation, he said the EU was ready to work with Dhaka to ensure a smooth and successful transition while exploring the prospect of a future Free Trade Agreement (FTA).
The envoy said the offer to explore such an agreement with a country yet to graduate from LDC status was unprecedented for the European Union.
"The key message is: we are ready to match the level of speed and ambition demonstrated by Bangladesh," he said.
He, however, said the two sides would first have to determine whether sufficient common ground existed for a balanced, reciprocal and mutually beneficial agreement.
The ambassador stressed the importance of ensuring a level playing field for businesses under any future trade arrangement.
He said the success of deeper Bangladesh-EU economic engagement would depend on strong and accountable institutions, rule of law, labour rights, human rights, environmental protection and good governance. "These issues are central; they are not peripheral," he said.
The EU envoy said Bangladesh was navigating an important phase in its development journey amid LDC graduation, political transition, economic pressure, climate vulnerability and an increasingly complex external environment.
He said stronger institutions, independent oversight mechanisms and predictable and inclusive decision-making would help Bangladesh withstand geopolitical, geoeconomic, climate, social and technological pressures.
The ambassador also underlined the importance of constitutional reform, greater political consensus, skilled human resources, green growth, diversified exports and reliable infrastructure for the country's future development.
"If this country is to attract investment, both foreign and domestic, and to create meaningful jobs for its youth, it will require strong institutions and oversight mechanisms," he said.
He said critical infrastructure needed to be safeguarded while data management should remain transparent.
Highlighting the EU's investment approach, the envoy said European engagement sought to combine investment with technology, international standards, long-term capital and innovation.
He cited the Laldia Container Terminal in Chittagong and green bond initiatives as examples of areas where European engagement could bring additional value.
The ambassador said the EU could also share its experience in public administration and political and economic transition with Bangladesh.
He said Europe itself had gone through major transformations from autocratic systems towards democratic governance and modern economic institutions.
The EU, he said, wanted to help Bangladesh navigate increasing global competition while remaining "open, sovereign, resilient and connected".
Earlier in his speech, the envoy said the EU's own response to growing global uncertainty had been to strengthen its strategic autonomy while remaining open, cooperative and committed to international law and multilateralism.
He said the EU sought partnerships based on mutual interest, respect, fairness and a level playing field, while offering rules-based trade, sustainable investment and cooperation in climate, connectivity, digital transformation and human development.

The meeting decided to strengthen patrols at key points along waterways and maintain 24-hour surveillance through control rooms.

item.title: American Deisseroth, Germans Hegemann and Nagel win 2026 Nobel medicine prize for brain research
item.description:
SWEDEN-NOBEL-AWARD-MEDICINE-PHYSIOLOGY

Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for "discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics," the award-giving body said on Monday.

Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.

Optogenetics "makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain," the prize-givers said.

"This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries."

The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days.

The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel's will and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited interruptions, chiefly during the World War One and World War Two.

A sixth award, the economics prize, was established in 1968 by Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank.

The medicine prize has honoured some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past century, including Alexander Fleming's work on penicillin, recognised in 1945, and Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups.

Last year, American scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan's Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer.

Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in Oslo, a tradition often linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel's lifetime.

More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their longstanding traditions.

The celebrations culminate on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden's and Norway's royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honour.

item.title: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
item.description:
YEMEN-SAUDI-ISRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The government’s armed forces would press the offensive “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. A military spokesman later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons.

The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen’s capital Sanaa and vast parts of the northwest, where most of the population live, since 2014. They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies, and have updated their weaponry with the help of Iran.

The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and some 150 km (90 miles) of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route.

That advance also opened a new front in the wider US-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran’s responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

Bangladesh condemns Houthi drone attack on Madinah infrastructure

Houthis say they struck Saudi Arabia

As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council, made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia.

They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.

Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted.

He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen's regional allies and international partners to support PLC forces and institutions.

Regional and western officials had told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.

Houthis say struck oil facility near Riyadh, as Saudis hit Sanaa

New front in Mideast war

The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.

The United States’ war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East and depleted crucial military hardware.

Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups and factions backed by competing regional and international actors.

After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi’ite Muslims, captured Sanaa.

The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also recognised by the United Nations, has since the Houthi takeover controlled the south and east of the country, based in the former South Yemen capital of Aden.

Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis.

A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

Saudi plans Houthi offensive with 100,000 Yemeni troops, US, other countries' support

Houthis on front foot

The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast.

Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.

The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.

Three in four ​families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, ‌which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

item.title: House rents rise 27pc in 4 years, taking a bigger bite out of incomes
item.description:
Shahadat Hossain works for a private company in the capital. He earns a total of Tk 39,000 a month. Until recently, he lived in a shared rented accommodation. He recently got married and now needs a small flat, preferably close to his office in Mohammadpur.

Over the past week, he has searched extensively for a two-room flat in Adabor, Shekhertek and areas around the Mohammadpur bus stand. But the rents are beyond his means, with nothing available for less than Tk 18,000.

If he rents a flat at this rate, gas and electricity bills will be added to the rent, along with a service charge. Altogether, the monthly cost would exceed Tk 20,000.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Sunday, Shahadat Hossain said, “If half my salary goes towards housing, how am I supposed to manage in this high-cost market?”

Expressing his helplessness, he said he had been forced to decide to look for cheaper accommodation much farther from his office. Although this would make commuting more difficult, he said it would save some money to cover other expenses.

Like Shahadat, almost all people in Dhaka on limited and fixed incomes face a similar situation. A large portion of their income has to be spent on housing. Even then, they cannot always find a home that meets their needs. Moreover, once a house is rented, most landlords increase the rent almost every year.

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), house rents in the country have increased by around 27 per cent over the past four years. In reality, however, rents are rising at a faster rate than the government’s figures suggest. The increase has been particularly sharp in Dhaka.

Four years ago, Fozayel Ahmed rented a three-room flat in East Goran for Tk 20,000. He said the rent has now risen to Tk 27,000. It has been increased three times, meaning a 35 per cent rise.

Electricity and gas bills have also increased during this period. He has had to cut back on other expenses to cover the additional costs.

The United Nations Economic and Social Council’s World Urbanization Prospects 2025 report says around 36.6 million people now live in Dhaka city and its surrounding areas. Dhaka is the world’s second-most populous city.

A large proportion of this vast population lives in rented accommodation. The government enacted the House Rent Control Act in 1991, but the law has remained largely ineffective. This is because regulations needed to enforce the law have still not been formulated. It is against this backdrop that World Habitat Day is being observed today, Monday.

However, he said there is no mechanism to monitor whether the increase is reasonable or whether excessive costs are being imposed on tenants. For this, it is essential to formulate regulations under the House Rent Control Act. This would make it possible to resolve rent-related disputes within a legal framework.

Additional house rent: Law on paper, not in reality

How much have rents increased?

Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) publishes a house rent index every three months. According to the government agency, house rents in Bangladesh increased by around 27 per cent between July 2022 and the end of July 2026.

This is the national average. Rents have increased even more depending on demand and location. In Dhaka, for example, both the ammount of rents and the rate of increase are the highest.

In different areas of Dhaka, rents for three-room flats ranged from Tk 18,000 to Tk 50,000. A monthly service charge of Tk 3,000 to Tk 7,000 is added to this.

Over the past two days, Prothom Alo surveyed house rents in Mirpur, Mohammadpur, Shekhertek, Moghbazar, Eskaton, Paribagh, Banasree, Jatrabari and Bashundhara Residential Area in the capital.

In these areas, rents for three-room flats ranged from Tk 18,000 to Tk 50,000. A monthly service charge of Tk 3,000 to Tk 7,000 is added to this. However, rents are somewhat lower in areas farther from the main roads. For example, two-room flats in Basila, Mohammadpur, can be rented for between Tk 10,000 and Tk 15,000.

Ahsan Habib has been renting a house in the Shewrapara area of the capital for five years. He told Prothom Alo that the rent had been increased twice during this period. His landlord has informed him that it will be raised by another Tk 1,000 from January.

Tenants complain that in most cases, landlords and tenants do not have a written agreement. As a result, landlords put pressure on tenants to increase the rent at any time, often verbally.

In its 2022 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, BBS provided an average estimate of how much households spend on different items.

According to BBS, the average monthly income of a household in Bangladesh is Tk 32,422, while its expenditure is Tk 31,500. Some 42 per cent of expenditure goes towards food. The second-largest category of expenditure is house rent along with gas, electricity and water bills.

Experts say most people come to Dhaka primarily in search of work. If transport links were better, many could live outside Dhaka. This would reduce pressure on housing and help keep rents under control.

He said Bangladesh will import LNG and fertiliser from Algeria under the G2G framework.
Salahuddin also urged Algeria to widen the trade basket in Dhaka's favour, saying Algiers could increase imports of Bangladeshi garments and pharmaceutical products.
Salahuddin further called on Algeria to hire skilled workers from Bangladesh, including doctors and nurses.
Beyond trade and energy, the two sides discussed maintaining peace and order, security cooperation, preventing and combating human trafficking, migration management, and expanding economic and commercial ties.
They laid particular emphasis on specialised training to improve the efficiency and professionalism of security forces, joint workshops, and the exchange of legislative support.
Recalling that Algeria was the first Arab country to recognise Bangladesh after its independence in 1971, the ambassador voiced his country's strong interest in further strengthening the historic and friendly relationship.
Referring to the invitation extended by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the Algerian President to visit Dhaka, Salahuddin said Bangladesh is pleased that the invitation has been accepted.
He stressed fixing a mutually convenient diplomatic date for the visit.
At the end of the meeting, both countries reaffirmed their commitment to deepening and strengthening cooperation in security, trade and bilateral diplomatic relations.

item.title: Two Indian nationals shot in BSF firing at Kurigram border
item.description:
Two Indian nationals were seriously injured after the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) allegedly opened fire on them along the Daikhawa border in Ulipur upazila of Kurigram on Sunday afternoon.
The injured men were identified as Ismail Hossain, 35, and Khaja Abdul Alim, 39, residents of Barobalu village under Sukchar Police Station in Assam’s South Salmara-Mankachar district.
After being shot, they crossed into Bangladesh and were rescued by local residents, who took them to a clinic in Rangpur. Later, the Detective Branch (DB) of Rangpur Metropolitan Police transferred them to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for better treatment.
Rangpur Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner and DB chief Sanatan Chakraborty confirmed the matter to Dhaka Tribune, saying the two men were arrested in a case filed over illegal entry into Bangladesh.
Doctors found multiple pellet wounds on their bodies, while one of them also sustained a burn-like injury.
The circumstances surrounding their presence in the border area remain unclear. DB officials are investigating the incident, including why the BSF allegedly opened fire on the two Indian nationals.
Local residents suspect the men had crossed into the border area to smuggle cattle and were shot by the BSF after being mistaken for Bangladeshi cattle smugglers.
The injured men, however, claimed they had gone to a char area near the border to graze cattle. They alleged that BSF personnel detained them and tried to push them into Bangladesh.
According to the men, they resisted, leading to a scuffle, after which the BSF allegedly opened fire and left them injured on the Bangladesh side.
Khaja Abdul Alim, one of the injured men, said they were Indian citizens and had gone to the char to graze cattle. He alleged that BSF personnel accused them of being Bangladeshi cattle smugglers and took them to a char area, where an argument broke out before they were shot.
He appealed to the governments of Bangladesh and India to facilitate their return home.
Police and local residents said the BSF personnel fired at Ismail and Khaja from an area near Assam’s Narayanpur land port towards Daikhawar Char in the Brahmaputra River area of Ulipur.

item.title: US-German trio wins Nobel Prize in Medicine for work on optogenetics
item.description:
The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviors like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
The trio were honored “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells,” the Nobel Assembly said.
Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in a brain.
They have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.
In clinical medicine, the method is being used in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment, and may one day lead to treatments for disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.
“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
The secretary general of the assembly, Thomas Perlmann, told reporters he was able to reach the three laureates by phone to break the news.
“That was great to talk to them. I first called Deisseroth he was very tired when he answered. He was definitely asleep, but he woke up,” he said.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel were examining why a single-celled alga was able to swim toward a light source.
They discovered an algal protein with unique properties, called channelrhodopsin, found on the surface of the cell.
When illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein.
Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that any cell they put the protein in became light sensitive.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats.
By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal.
He published his breakthrough in 2005, and two years later, made the light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
In 2021, Deisseroth and Hegemann won the Lasker Prize for their work in the field, often considered a precursor to the Nobel.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin.
Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg.
The Nobel prize for physics will be announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
Some pundits have suggested that for literature, the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Central or Latin America.
Argentine author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.
Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize -- the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.
This year, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.
Among possible laureates this year are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.
Others include Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
This year’s laureates will receive their prizes -- a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2-million cheque -- on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of the prize’s creator, scientist Alfred Nobel.

item.title: Net govt borrowing rises by Tk13,000cr
item.description:
The government's reliance on bank borrowing to finance its operating and development expenditure has grown further.
From the beginning of the current FY27, significant pressure appeared in budget income-and-expenditure accounts—a strain that has become more evident over time.
With domestic revenue collection falling short of target and foreign disbursement slowing down, the government has ultimately had to rely on banks to meet its spending needs.
This has directly impacted public bank borrowing: in just the first two months of the fiscal year, government bank borrowing grew more than 5-fold compared to the same period last year.
According to updated data from Bangladesh Bank, the government borrowed Tk16,601 crore from commercial banks in July and August of the current fiscal.
During the same period of the previous fiscal year, this figure was Tk3,256 crore.
This means commercial bank borrowing by the government grew by more than 5 times year-on-year.
However, during the same period, the government repaid a portion of its outstanding loans from Bangladesh Bank.
After paying back Tk3,728 crore to the central bank in July–August, the government's net borrowing from the overall banking system stood at Tk12,872 crore for this period.
The government has set a target to borrow Tk112,000 crore from the banking system in the current FY27.
In just the first two months, net borrowing has already reached 11.49% of that target.
In contrast, during the same period last fiscal year, the government made net repayments to the banking system rather than taking on new debt.
Consequently, this early borrowing surge points to added pressure on government financial management.
Economists and bankers attribute the rising bank debt primarily to sluggish revenue collection and growing government expenditure.
Value Added Tax (VAT) collection dropped by nearly 20 percent year-on-year in the first two months of the fiscal year.
Changes to VAT filing rules also impacted revenue flows: after transitioning from monthly payments to a quarterly scheme, efforts are now underway to reinstate monthly VAT collection.
On the other hand, while revenue fell, government spending did not.
The government has had to spend on the new pay scale for public employees, energy sector costs and subsidies, and various development projects.
As a result, reliance on bank borrowing to bridge the deficit has increased.
With weak credit demand in the private sector, banks currently hold relatively high liquidity.
As private sector credit growth dipped below 5%, banks increased their investments in government Treasury bills and bonds.
Bankers state that for now, higher government borrowing is not creating major crowding-out pressure on the private sector.
However, declining interest rates on government securities are squeezing bank earnings, with yields in some cases falling below deposit rates.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, as of August 30, the government's total outstanding debt to commercial banks reached Tk608,025 crore, up from Tk591,424 crore at the end of June.
Meanwhile, outstanding debt to Bangladesh Bank fell from Tk94,051 crore in June to Tk90,322 crore in August.
Taken together, the government's total outstanding debt to the banking sector stands at nearly Tk700,000 crore.

item.title: Savings certificate sales surge 57% in two months
item.description:
Interest in investing in savings certificates (Sanchayapatra) is on the rise. In July and August of the current FY27, savings certificate sales reached Tk2,463.12 crore.
During the same period of the previous fiscal year, sales stood at Tk1,572.29 crore.
This marks a nearly 57% increase in sales over the two-month period compared to a year earlier.
According to data from the National Savings Directorate, along with the two-month total, August also saw significant growth. In August of this year, savings certificates worth Tk403.65 crore were sold.
In the same month of 2025, sales were Tk278.81 crore. Year-on-year sales for August grew by Tk124.84 crore, or approximately 45%.
Stakeholders attribute the rising interest to higher returns compared to bank deposits.
Profit rates on savings certificates were also revised for new investments between July 1 and December 31 of this year.
However, despite the jump in gross sales, savings certificates have yet to become a major source of net borrowing for the government.
A substantial portion of new sales is being spent on repaying the principal to existing investors.
In FY26, total savings certificate sales reached Tk92,513 crore, while Tk92,077 crore was paid out to clear principal on matured certificates.
Consequently, net government borrowing from savings certificates during that fiscal year stood at just Tk436.06 crore.
In contrast, the budget targeted borrowing Tk12,500 crore from this sector, which was later revised down to Tk11,500 crore.
Just a few years ago, savings certificates were a primary source of internal government borrowing.
In FY21, net government borrowing from this sector was nearly Tk42,000 crore.
Today, because most incoming investments are channeled back into paying principal and interest to previous investors, the net funds remaining with the government are considerably lower.
By the end of August 2026, total customer investment in savings certificates—representing the government's outstanding debt in this sector—stood at Tk336,465 crore, up from Tk333,846 crore in August of the previous year.

item.title: Remittance inflows up over 15% in current FY27
item.description:
Bangladesh has received $8.798 billion in remittances so far in FY27, sent to the country between July 1 and October 3.
This represents a 15.1% increase compared to the $7.643 billion received during the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Executive spokesperson of Bangladesh Bank Arief Hossain Khan confirmed the data on Sunday (October 4).
He noted that the significant growth in remittances was driven by an increase in funds sent home by Bangladeshi expatriate workers during the first few months of the current fiscal year.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, the country’s gross foreign exchange reserves stood at approximately $36.14 billion as of September 29.
Earlier on September 20, total foreign exchange reserves were at $36.30 billion.
According to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) BPM6 calculation method at that time, the reserve amount was $31.45 billion.
According to the central bank's updated report, remittances worth $1.877 billion arrived in the country during the first 20 days of September.
Of this, expatriates sent $130 million in just three days—from September 17 to 19—compared to $1.869 billion received in the first 19 days of September last year.

item.title: Turkiye, Pakistan to deploy forces to Saudi amid Houthi attacks
item.description:
Turkiye and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defense alliance, the three countries said Monday, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The three countries in August signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.
The pact unites Nato’s second-largest army, that of Turkiye, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular ones targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.
The trio “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity,” they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom.”
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Monday launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis say struck Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
item.description:
SAUDI-YEMEN-IRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

Iran-backed Houthis said Monday they had struck Riyadh’s international airport, an oil refinery and other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.

Pakistan and Turkey have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.

The fighting in Yemen has become the most active front in the Middle East war in recent weeks, displacing more than 184,000 people, the United Nations says, and deepening the conflict that has engulfed the wider region.

The Houthis previously controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the western city of Hodeida, but seized swathes of coastline last month along the Red Sea and key Bab al-Mandab Strait, in Yemen’s deadliest fighting in years.

The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.

The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.

Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit “military targets” belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.

They “destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines” and had “thwarted a planned attack” targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.

Later, the military said it had driven the Houthis from the area surrounding the Bab al-Mandeb Strait—a vital route for maritime traffic—including the port city of Mocha, Dhubab airport and Al-Omari military camp.

They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where deadly fighting has surged in recent days.

Military sources stopped short of confirming an official announcement of Mocha’s recapture, saying that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the port.

UN ‘deeply concerned’

Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Monday evening, with a Houthi spokesman saying the group had hit King Khalid International Airport, a refinery belonging to state oil giant Aramco and other targets in the kingdom’s south.

It came a day after Yemen’s government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory—home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event of any attack.

They also agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.

The statement did not specify what role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.

A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”, and condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia.

Houthi attacks have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.

A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom’s exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.

Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.

Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.

“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
item.description:
Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month, but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Niño pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary "electrification" pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
"In many ways, the defining contexts for this year's climate summit will be heat and Hormuz," said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting November 9, said this year's extreme events "show climate change is not a future challenge".
"It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising," he said.
A "pre-COP" meeting began Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders' retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Unlike recent COPs -- where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels -- the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
"Much of the Antalya summit will be a 'roll up the sleeves' effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year," Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels -- the leading cause of climate change.
Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At last year's summit, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
"Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment," Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere.
Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phaseout conference without UN involvement this year.
France, the Netherlands and Germany have published "roadmaps" with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations: "No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward," he said.
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
"Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail," said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an "action agenda" alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% on Tuesday to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put "a huge amount of pressure" on western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
"We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it," Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said.

Student protests rock French; police fire teargas, arrest 6,100
item.description:
FRANCE-PROTEST/

Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools on Tuesday as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the biggest day of action in a wave of demonstrations against understaffed and dilapidated classrooms.

In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs marked with "The state has killed national education" and other messages, in largely peaceful rallies. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.

But in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

"There is such a gap between the elites and us," said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.

The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide, presenting a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's cash-strapped government at a time when it faces strong economic headwinds.

The High School Students Union said more than half of France's high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.

"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," said Roberta, another recent high-school graduate at a protest outside Paris' prestigious Henri IV school.

Schools were facing a list of problems from water leaks to rat infestations, she added.

Thousands of arrests

The government has responded to the demonstrations with riot police.

Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.

At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.

A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.

"They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris.

"If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake," he added.

Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. LFI denies the accusation.

Prime minister promises a response

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.

The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.

Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government's words were not enough. "That's all fine and dandy, but that's not what's going to change the daily lives of our children," she said.

Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.

The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.

The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

item.title: Latest attack on civil and political rights of Bangladesh citizens: HRW
item.description:
The mass arrest of attendees at a small left-wing party’s meeting in Dhaka on 26 September is the latest incident in the Bangladesh authorities’ ongoing assault on civil and political rights, according to a report run on the website of Human Rights Watch (HRW).

Police took around 290 supporters of the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal into custody after members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s youth wing – the Jubo Dal – claimed the gathering was a 'secret' meeting of the former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, whose activities are currently banned.

A court remanded 27 of those arrested to custody, because it was alleged they had chanted the slogan 'Joy Bangla' (Victory to Bengal), a slogan associated with the Awami League.

The Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal was part of a 14-party alliance, led by the Awami League, that governed Bangladesh from 2009 until 2024, when it was toppled by student led protests in which hundreds were killed by security forces.

The current ruling party, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), faced severe repression under the Awami League government. Since being elected in February, it has targeted its own perceived opponents with arbitrary detention and hundreds of Awami League members are currently in jail, mostly without charge.

Police have repeatedly raided alleged gatherings of Awami League supporters.

On 26 September, the same day as the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal meeting, police in Barisal detained 12 Awami League activists for allegedly holding a 'secret' meeting to 'plan sabotage', two days later, 15 were arrested in Dhaka under the Anti-Terrorism Act on similar allegations.

In both cases those detained said they had gathered to mark Sheikh Hasina’s birthday.

During Sheikh Hasina’s authoritarian rule, there were widespread and grave rights violations—including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, torture and the arbitrary detention of political opponents.

The Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power promising to restore human rights and the rule of law. Instead, the new government has arbitrarily detained perceived opponents and rolled back human rights safeguards the interim government proposed.

International human rights law guarantees freedoms of expression and association for all. Past violations of those rights committed when Awami League was in power cannot justify the Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s current violations of the same rights. Bangladeshi history is rife with examples of where such repression can lead.

item.title: Bangladesh to buy 10 aircraft from Airbus, deal tomorrow
item.description:
After Boeing, the government is now set to purchase 10 aircraft from European aircraft manufacturer Airbus. A deal between state-owned Biman Bangladesh Airlines and Airbus will be signed tomorrow, Wednesday.

According to a statement issued by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the signing ceremony, titled 'Spreading Our Wings Together,' will be held at a hotel in the capital. Neither Bangladesh nor Airbus has yet disclosed how much the 10 aircraft will cost.

Under the proposed agreement, Biman will purchase four A350-900s and six A321neos from Airbus. The wide-body A350-900s will primarily be used on long-haul international routes, while the narrow-body A321neos will be deployed on regional and medium-haul routes.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said Airbus could begin delivering the aircraft in 2033. The aircraft could be added to Biman’s fleet in phases through 2036 or 2037.

25 more aircraft to come from Boeing

Before signing the deal with Airbus, Biman signed two separate agreements this year to purchase a total of 25 aircraft from US aircraft manufacturer Boeing.

In the first deal, signed on 30 April, Biman agreed to purchase 14 aircraft for about USD 3.7 billion (approximately Tk 454 billion). The order includes eight 787-10 Dreamliners, two 787-9s and four 737-8s.

In the second deal, signed in New York on 23 September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Biman agreed to purchase another 11 aircraft. These include five 787-10s and six 737-8 MAX aircraft.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said deliveries of the Boeing aircraft could begin in 2031. It will take 11 to 12 years to receive all the aircraft.

The ministry said Biman will not have to make payments immediately after the agreements are signed. Payment will be made when each aircraft is delivered. However, Biman authorities have requested that at least one aircraft be delivered in 2027 or 2028.

Biman’s current fleet

Biman currently has 19 aircraft in its fleet, including 14 Boeing aircraft and five Dash 8s.

However, two aircraft in the fleet are close to becoming unserviceable. The remaining 17 are also expected to be phased out within the next few years. To meet immediate demand, Biman is therefore trying to lease 10 more aircraft. Despite several attempts, the state-owned airline has yet to lease any aircraft.

Once Airbus’ 10 aircraft and the 25 Boeing aircraft under contract are added, Biman will have 35 new aircraft in the coming years. Including its current 19 aircraft, the airline’s fleet will exceed 50 aircraft.

According to Biman, of the 35 new aircraft, 19 will be wide-body aircraft and 16 will be narrow-body aircraft.

Most of Biman’s current fleet is made up of aircraft manufactured by US-based Boeing. With the addition of Airbus aircraft, Biman Bangladesh Airlines will, for the first time, operate a fleet comprising aircraft from both US and European manufacturers.

item.title: PM Tarique to visit Japan, manpower deal on cards
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to visit Japan on October 26 for a four-day official trip, with Dhaka and Tokyo working to finalise a manpower agreement that could emerge as one of the key outcomes of his first bilateral visit to the country.
The October 26-29 visit will take place at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, according to Foreign Ministry and diplomatic sources.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold bilateral talks in Tokyo, while Tarique is also expected to meet Emperor Naruhito.
The dates and planned visit were also reported by multiple diplomatic sources on Tuesday.
Officials said manpower exports, Japanese investment, trade and energy cooperation are expected to feature prominently in the talks, as the two countries seek to deepen their Strategic Partnership.
Several memorandums of understanding and agreements are being discussed ahead of the visit, diplomatic sources said.
Among them, an MoU related to sending Bangladeshi workers to Japan is at an advanced stage of negotiations and could be signed during the prime minister’s visit if the two sides reach final agreement.
The manpower issue gives the visit particular significance as Bangladesh seeks to expand access to Japan’s labour market amid Tokyo’s growing demand for foreign workers.
Japan announced last year that it planned to recruit at least 100,000 Bangladeshi workers over five years.
Bangladesh and Japan also signed two MoUs in Tokyo in May 2025 aimed at developing skilled manpower for the Japanese market.
Since then, Dhaka has sought to accelerate recruitment by expanding Japanese-language and technical training and addressing procedural barriers facing Bangladeshi workers.
The government has also established a dedicated Japan Cell under the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment.
The ministry says Bangladesh plans to send 100,000 workers to Japan annually in response to Japanese demand, with opportunities primarily under the Technical Intern Training Programme, Specified Skilled Worker scheme and professional employment categories.
Tarique himself has made expansion of the Japanese labour market a priority.
During a meeting with a special adviser to the Japanese prime minister in July, he urged Tokyo to recruit more skilled Bangladeshi workers and sought greater Japanese cooperation in skills development and investment.
The upcoming visit is therefore expected to review progress on those initiatives and explore ways to translate existing commitments into greater numbers of Bangladeshi workers entering Japan.
The invitation for Tarique to visit Japan was formally conveyed on behalf of Takaichi during recent high-level exchanges between the two governments.
The Japanese side reiterated the invitation during bilateral consultations, while Bangladesh invited Takaichi to visit Dhaka at a mutually convenient time.
Foreign Ministry officials said the two prime ministers would discuss ways to expand economic cooperation, with Bangladesh particularly interested in attracting further Japanese investment.
Japan is already one of Bangladesh’s major development partners and has been involved in large infrastructure projects, while the two countries have increasingly sought to move the relationship beyond traditional development assistance towards trade, investment, skills and strategic cooperation.

item.title: Belgium's Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize
item.description:
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen on Tuesday won the Nobel physics prize for groundbreaking work using South Pole ice to capture neutrinos originating in the distant cosmos, providing insight into the far reaches of space.
“This year’s prize is about ghostly messengers from space,” Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference.
Halzen was honored “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” the jury said.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Halzen’s work had been fundamental for the observatory -- “a cubic kilometer of ice that is equipped with light sensors” -- and has “paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.”
Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos -- rare subatomic particles -- “from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe.”
Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States, where he is a citizen.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” he told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced.
“But it’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize,” Halzen said.
The academy explained that high energy neutrinos are created in the same environments as other particles.
“However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way,” it said in a statement.
Halzen first presented his idea for the observatory in 1988 and his idea quickly gained the support of other researchers.
Preliminary testing was conducted just a few years later but the observatory was not completed until 2011.
“Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions,” the jury explained.
“For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project,” Halzen said.
The award is the second Nobel of the season, after the medicine prize was awarded on Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The researchers were honored for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics, which involves controlling nerve signals with light.
Last year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Briton John Clarke, Frenchman Michel Devoret and American John Martinis for putting quantum mechanics into action and enabling the development of all kinds of digital technology from cellphones to a new generation of computers.
The physics prize will be followed by the chemistry one on Wednesday.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award -- the peace prize -- is due on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize -- and Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal -- and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12-million-kronor ($1.2-million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll rises to 1,134 as 6 children die 24hrs
item.description:
Six more children died with measles-like symptoms in 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,134 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all six latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,032, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 102, it said.
A total of 1,291 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24 hours, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 199,013
